title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for residential cleaning
audience: Solo residential cleaners and small cleaning teams who want more work from households and businesses that fit their suburbs, their route and their job size.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a client need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide what work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Write down the home types you clean well (for example, a three-bedroom home on a fortnightly route), the price range you can sustain, the postcodes you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each client needs you. A fortnightly home on a route you already run is worth more to a small business than a one-off deep clean across town. If you cannot state these criteria, you cannot tell a good lead from a poor one. Business.gov.au suggests writing one short profile for each customer segment (24 September 2024).

instruction.heading: Reach households through channels they already use
instruction.body: Households mostly come through referrals from existing clients and local recommendations. Councils publish directories of local business networks and referral groups, such as the Wyndham City directory (undated). Business Victoria suggests testing your assumptions about buyers with interviews and simple research before you commit (undated). Do not build a list of householders from private address or property data, and do not turn up at a home to make an offer. Public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules (OAIC).

instruction.heading: Score prospects against written criteria
instruction.body: Keep one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit. For households, the criteria are postcode, route, home type and repeat need. For a business, add whether there is a decision-maker you can reach and whether the job falls within your insurance. Record the date and the source of each contact detail. Do not buy or scrape lists: ACMA says that buying a list does not remove the duty to show consent.

instruction.heading: Use public signals only for businesses and public bodies
instruction.body: Public signals are weak for household cleaning. Some councils publish planning permit registers, and the City of Casey register on the Victorian open-data portal is one example (metadata published 15 November 2023). Check your own council's register. Building permit data suits area-level planning rather than individual contact (DataVic, 28 August 2026). Do not use any signal to target a private person.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A first message says how you came to know about the business or notice, makes one observation you can verify, and offers one small next step, such as a written quote for a defined area or a short call. Keep it honest and short. The ACCC found in July 2026 that many unsolicited approaches were pressured or misleading, and that many salespeople did not identify themselves (ACCC, 28 July 2026). Identify yourself and make it easy to say no.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide in advance how many follow-ups you will send and how far apart they will be. Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and record the request with its date. ACMA says an unsubscribe must be honoured within five working days.

procedure: Write the home types, area, price range and repeat-need criteria for the work you want.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason and a source.
Choose the referral channels and any public signals you will use, and note the date each one is checked.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules, the Do Not Call Register and your licence and insurance before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of each month.

workedExamples.situation: A solo cleaner covers three suburbs (illustrative). A public notice goes up about planned repairs to the common areas of a 12-apartment block in one of them. The property manager's business email address is on the agency's website.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the cleaner send a sales message to the property manager now, and what should it contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: The block is a business prospect inside the service area, so it fits the criteria better than a one-off job across town. The cleaner does not send a sales email just because the address is published. ACMA says publishing a business address does not by itself permit commercial messages, so the cleaner first checks whether the manager has agreed to receive messages or has invited contact. If not, the cleaner checks the Do Not Call Register before any phone call. The DNCR guide gives calling hours of weekdays 9am to 8pm and Saturdays 9am to 5pm (2018 copyright notice; check for updates). The first contact names the notice, says how the business learned of it, offers one defined item, such as a written quote for the common areas, and asks one question. The cleaner does not contact individual residents or enter the common area without an invitation.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong fits.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about a household to make contact.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person gave you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Pitching a service the cleaner is not insured to deliver.
commonErrors.prevention: Check insurance before outreach. Licence and insurance rules were not researched, so check your state's rules.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a licensed or authorised service in outreach unless you hold the licence that the state or territory where the work is done requires. This lesson does not grant any licence. Licence rules for house cleaning were not researched, so check the rule for each state or territory you work in.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA says marketing messages need consent, that consent must be recorded, and that an unsubscribe must be honoured within five working days. The Act's text was not read for this lesson.
Check every telephone number against the Do Not Call Register before a telemarketing call. The 2018 DNCR industry guide sets the calling hours; check for any update before use.

Public information does not by itself permit contact. The OAIC says public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules. Whether the Privacy Act applies to a small business depends on its turnover and other factors, and that coverage was not confirmed.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added.
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen.
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned.
summary: Define the homes and businesses you want before you look for them.
Use referrals, local networks and business signals. Never build contact lists from private information.
Gap: no Australian source on residential client sources or conversion rates was found.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should you contact first?
options: A one-off job well outside your service area, because it looks large
A property manager with several buildings inside your service area that you already visit
Any business with a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A notice shows planned works at a building in your area. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Message each resident using their private contact details
Contact the building's manager by a route that the electronic message and do-not-call rules allow
Go into the common area to look and ask the crew what they are doing

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what must you do?
options: Make the subject line as catchy as possible
Ask the prospect to like your social page first
Confirm the consent and unsubscribe requirements in current ACMA guidance

sourceReferences: business.gov.au, 'How to identify your target market', https://business.gov.au/marketing/how-to-identify-your-target-market, 24 September 2024. Supports: write one short profile for each customer segment.

Business Victoria, 'Who is my customer?', https://www.business.vic.gov.au/marketing-and-sales/increasing-sales-through-marketing/who-is-my-customer, no date shown. Victoria. Supports: test assumptions about buyers before committing; talk to likely buyers.

Wyndham City Council, 'Wyndham business networks', https://www.wyndham.vic.gov.au/node/320, no date shown. Victoria. Supports: councils publish directories of local business networks and referral groups.

ACMA, 'Spam: Industry obligations', https://www.acma.gov.au/theACMA/spam-industry-obligations, last updated 28 March 2019 (older source). Supports: marketing messages need consent; an unsubscribe must work for at least 30 days and be honoured within 5 business days; publishing a business address does not by itself permit commercial messages; buying a list does not remove the duty to show consent.

OAIC, 'Chapter 7: APP 7 direct marketing', https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/australian-privacy-principles/australian-privacy-principles-guidelines/chapter-7-app-7-direct-marketing, page modified 16 October 2023; version 1.1 dated 22 July 2019 (older source). Supports: public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules.

DataVic, 'Planning Permit Application Register' (City of Casey), https://discover.data.vic.gov.au/dataset/planning-permit-application-register, metadata published 15 November 2023, last updated 5 November 2026 as shown. Victoria. Supports: some councils publish registers of planning applications with suburb and status; check your own council's register.

DataVic, 'Building Permit Activity Data', https://discover.data.vic.gov.au/dataset/d397f0bc-d69b-4093-b8d5-d8daae4f73a3, last updated 28 August 2026. Victoria. Supports: permit records can be filtered by suburb or postcode, so they suit area-level decisions rather than individual contact. Owner and builder fields were not confirmed.

ACCC, 'Misleading and high pressure unsolicited sales practices widespread', https://www.accc.gov.au/media-release/misleading-and-high-pressure-unsolicited-sales-practices-widespread, 28 July 2026. Supports: many unsolicited approaches were pressured or misleading, and many salespeople did not identify themselves.

Do Not Call Register, 'DNCR industry guide', https://www.donotcall.gov.au/media/1212/dncr-industry-guide.pdf, 2018 copyright notice (older source). Supports: telemarketing to registered numbers is limited to weekdays 9am to 8pm and Saturdays 9am to 5pm, not Sundays or public holidays; lists should be checked against the register.

ACMA, 'Avoid sending spam', https://www.acma.gov.au/avoid-sending-spam, no date shown; read 2026-11-04 per the research file. Supports: consent, accurate sender details, and an unsubscribe honoured within five working days.
Notes: the DNCR calling hours come from a 2018 guide (older source). The residential example is illustrative. The Wyndham and Business Victoria pages are undated.

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam (ACMA)
officialReferences.covers: As recorded in the research files: consent is needed before marketing messages are sent; sender details must be accurate; each commercial message needs an unsubscribe that is honoured within five working days. Publisher: ACMA.
